content: The 2019 Web Annex E of the Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services, published by the World Health Organization (WHO), provides a detailed analysis of HIV testing strategy performance and its implications for global guideline development. The document emphasizes the importance of achieving a positive predictive value (PPV) of greater than 99% for HIV testing strategies in all settings. To meet this standard, the 2015 WHO guidelines recommended two consecutive reactive HIV tests for diagnosis in high-prevalence settings (HIV prevalence >5%) and three consecutive reactive tests in low-prevalence settings (HIV prevalence ≤5%). As HIV awareness and treatment coverage have improved, and HIV incidence has declined, the positivity rate among clients undergoing HIV testing has dropped below 5%, even in traditionally high-prevalence settings. This shift necessitates a reevaluation of testing strategies. Countries currently using the high-prevalence two-test strategy are encouraged to consider transitioning to a three-assay strategy for HIV diagnosis. A probability model was developed to simulate HIV testing outcomes for both highand low-prevalence strategies as outlined in the 2015 WHO guidelines. The model assumed a sensitivity of 99% and specificity of 98% for each assay, which are the minimum thresholds required for WHO prequalification. The analysis evaluated the expected number of false-positive and false-negative results, the PPV, the number of assays used, and the associated costs. The findings revealed that the three-test strategy significantly reduced the number of false-positive misclassifications, from approximately 45 per 100,000 tests to fewer than 1 per 100,000 tests, across all positivity levels. The PPV of the three-test strategy consistently exceeded the 99% target, ensuring high diagnostic reliability. While the number of assays required for the first two tests (A1 and A2) remained unchanged, the number of third assays (A3) increased under the three-test strategy. However, the overall cost increase was modest, with program costs primarily driven by the number of first assays (A1) conducted. The interpretation of these findings suggests that the three-test strategy provides superior diagnostic accuracy at a relatively low incremental cost compared to the two-test strategy. Given the declining positivity rates, it is recommended that all countries adopt a unified three-assay strategy for HIV diagnosis, as per the latest WHO guidance released in 2019. The publication also highlights the importance of adhering to WHO licensing and citation guidelines when using or adapting the material. It underscores that the views expressed are those of the named authors and do not necessarily reflect WHO's official position. Additionally, the document serves as part of the WHO's broader effort to enhance transparency and provide evidence-based recommendations for HIV testing services.
